summary: An exception is a **run-time anomaly** (e.g. memory exhaustion, a file that cannot be opened, division by zero). Exception handling lets the program recover and keep its normal flow.

Mechanism: **try** (run code that may fail), **throw** (create and raise an exception object), **catch** (a handler whose type matches). An optional **finally** runs whether or not an exception is thrown.

Hierarchy: Object, then Throwable, which splits into **Exception** and **Error**. **Unchecked** = RuntimeException and its subclasses, plus Error and its subclasses. Every other exception is **checked**.

A checked exception must be **caught or declared** with `throws`. If nothing catches an exception, it **propagates** up to the caller, and the JVM's default handler stops the program if no one catches it.
With several catch blocks, they are tested in order and only the **first match** runs. Specific types must come before general ones.
Custom exceptions `extend Exception` (or a subclass of it) and usually define just their constructors, which call `super(message)`.
mustMemorise: Checked = everything else under Exception, e.g. `IOException`, `FileNotFoundException`, `ClassNotFoundException`, plain `Exception`. They must be caught or declared with `throws`.
Hierarchy chain: `Object → Throwable → Exception → RuntimeException → ArithmeticException …` and `Throwable → Error`.
The 3 methods: `getMessage()` (the message), `toString()` (short description = class name + ': ' + message), `printStackTrace()` (the trace of method calls).
The 2 constructors on the slide: `Exception()` and `Exception(String message)`.
Only the FIRST matching catch runs. Putting a catch for a superclass before a catch for its subclass is a **compile error**.
A catch for a checked exception that the try body can never throw is a **compile error**. `catch(Exception e)` is always allowed.
`finally` runs on a normal finish, on a caught exception, on an uncaught exception, and even after a `return`. **`System.exit()` skips it.**
An exception thrown inside a catch is NOT caught by the catch blocks next to it. `finally` still runs, then the new exception propagates.
Propagation: if an exception is not caught, the rest of that method is skipped and control returns to the caller, continuing up to main and then the JVM.

items.title: What an exception is
notes: Definition: an exception is a **run-time** anomaly that a program may detect.
Examples: memory exhaustion, an input file that cannot be opened, division by zero.
**Exception handlers** (recovery procedures) catch exceptions in order to recover.

items.title: 'error if numOfStudents = 0' does not throw
notes: `totalMarks / (double)numOfStudents` is **floating-point** division. Dividing by 0 does NOT throw; it gives `NaN` (0.0/0.0) or `Infinity` (verified).
So with 0 students this version prints `Average marks = NaN`. It does not crash.
Only **integer** division or `%` by zero throws `ArithmeticException: / by zero`.
Output `70.0`: a double always prints with `.0`.

items.title: Version 2: if + System.exit(0)
notes: This is old-style error handling: an `if` check, a message, then `System.exit(0)`, which ends the JVM immediately.
This is the 'before' version that try/catch improves on.

items.title: Try / Throw / Catch definitions
notes: **Try**: try to see if there is any exception.
**Throw**: the method creates (raises) an exception **object** holding the exception type and the program state.
**Catch**: the **JVM** looks for a handler whose type **matches** the exception thrown.

items.title: try/throw/catch/finally syntax
notes: `throw new ExceptionName("msg");` uses `throw` (singular) inside the body. `throws` (with an s) goes in the method header.
You can have one or more `catch(Type name)` blocks, then an optional `finally` that runs **regardless** of whether an exception was thrown.
Real Java: try must be followed by at least one catch OR a finally (`try{}finally{}` is legal).

items.title: Flow when there is no exception
notes: The whole try block runs, **every catch block is skipped**, and execution continues after try/catch.
Output: `Average marks = 70.0` then `End of program execution!`.

items.title: Flow when an exception is thrown
notes: The rest of the try block after the `throw` is **skipped**, control jumps to the matching catch, and then execution continues after the try/catch.
Output: the message `Error: no of students must not equal to 0!` then `End of program execution!`.

items.title: Exception hierarchy (memorise)
notes: Object → **Throwable** → Exception and Error. Under Exception: ClassNotFoundException, IOException, AWTException (checked), and **RuntimeException**.

RuntimeException subclasses: Arithmetic, ArrayStore, ClassCast, IllegalArgument (→ NumberFormat), IllegalMonitorState, IndexOutOfBounds (→ ArrayIndex…, StringIndex…), NegativeArraySize, NullPointer, Security.
The two circled branches are **Unchecked**: RuntimeException's subtree AND **Error**'s subtree (LinkageError, VirtualMachineError, AWTError).
Hollow-triangle arrows point UP to the parent class. The top of the tree is general, the bottom is specific.

items.title: Useful exceptions, and FileNotFoundException is CHECKED
notes: ArithmeticException = integer division by zero. Array/StringIndexOutOfBounds = index < 0 or **≥ length**. Both are subclasses of IndexOutOfBounds.
NullPointerException = using a null reference. NumberFormatException = `parseInt("abc")`. IllegalArgumentException = an improper argument.
Trap: `FileNotFoundException` is listed here but extends `IOException`, so it is **checked** (verified). Every other exception on the slide is unchecked.

items.title: Code that triggers each exception
notes: `array[5]` on `new int[5]` gives ArrayIndexOutOfBounds (valid indexes are 0 to 4).
`str.charAt(str.length())` gives StringIndexOutOfBounds. `Integer.parseInt("abc")` gives NumberFormatException.
Typos: `st.length()` should be `str.length()`, and the slide uses curly quotes. The intended result is a NullPointerException on the null `str`.

items.title: Exception class, and 'root of all exceptions'
notes: The 2 constructors are `Exception()` and `Exception(String message)`. `getMessage()` returns the message (`null` if none). `toString()` gives e.g. `java.lang.Exception: hi`. `printStackTrace()` prints the call trace.
Slide wrong: the real root is **Throwable** (slide 15). `Error` is not an Exception, so `catch(Exception e)` won't catch an Error.
Exam: for 'root of the Exception classes' per this slide, answer Exception. For 'the top of the hierarchy / what catches everything', answer Throwable.

items.title: printStackTrace output
notes: `3/0` with ints gives ArithmeticException. `getMessage()` is `/ by zero`.
The trace lists the **most recent call first**: method3, method2, method1, main.
`System.exit(0)` in the catch ends the program, so `return k` is never reached.

items.title: Checked exceptions
notes: Checked = exceptions that **can be analysed by the compiler**, e.g. IOException when reading a file.
There are 2 options: 1) **catch** it with try/catch in the method that threw it, or 2) **delay** handling by declaring it with a `throws` clause.
If you do neither, it is a compile error ('unreported exception … must be caught or declared to be thrown', verified).

items.title: Unchecked exceptions
notes: Unchecked = **not checked by the compiler**: any subclass of **RuntimeException** OR class **Error**.
**Error IS unchecked.** A common wrong answer is 'Error is checked'.
They are caused by actions like bad input (ArithmeticException, IndexOutOfBounds) and are usually avoided by careful programming, not by catching.

items.title: Uncaught exceptions and the catch-or-declare rule
notes: An uncaught unchecked exception goes to **Java's default exception handler**, which ends the program with a message that includes the exception class name.
RuntimeException/Error: catching is not required. Anything else: either **catch** it or **declare** it with `throws`.

Corollary (verified): a catch for a **checked** exception the try body can never throw (e.g. `catch(IOException e)` around `int x=1;`) is a **compile error**. Catching `Exception`, `Throwable`, `RuntimeException` or `Error` is always allowed.

items.title: Version 4: try/catch/finally in main
notes: `finally` prints `End of program execution!` in **both** cases (normal and exception).
`finally` even runs if the try block executes `return`. Only `System.exit()` (or the JVM dying) skips it.

items.title: throws ArithmeticException is optional
notes: `throws` in the header declares exceptions the method may throw **but does not catch**.
ArithmeticException is unchecked, so this `throws` is **documentation only**. The code compiles without it, and callers are not forced to catch it (verified).
For a checked exception (e.g. `throws IOException`) the declaration is **required**, and the caller must then catch it or declare it too.

items.title: 'Average marks = 70' should be 70.0
notes: `average` is a `double`, so Java prints `Average marks = 70.0`. The slide's `70` is wrong (slide 36 has the same mistake).
Also, the second prompt says 'Enter **the** number of students', but the code prints 'Enter number of students'.
Exam: real output is `70.0`.

items.title: Exception propagation (definition)
notes: If an exception is thrown and not caught by the handlers after its try block, control is **transferred to the calling method**, and so on up the call chain.
If main doesn't catch it either, the JVM default handler prints the stack trace and ends the program.

items.title: Propagation walk-through (steps 1-8)
notes: method3: `array[6]` on length 5 throws AIOOBE. `End method3()` is skipped.
method2 has no handler, so `End method2()` is also **skipped** and the exception moves up to method1.
method1's `catch(ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)` handles it. Then `End method1()` runs, and main prints `End of program execution` (back to normal).

items.title: Old-JDK exception message
notes: The slide shows `Exception message: 6` and `Java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: 6` (and the capital J is a typo).
JDK 11+ (verified on 17): `getMessage()` is `Index 6 out of bounds for length 5`, and the trace line starts `java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 6 out of bounds for length 5`.
The ORDER of lines is correct: Start×4 lines, message, trace (method3 first), End method1(), End of program. Note `End method2()`/`End method3()` never print.
Exam: focus on which lines print and in what order. If the question quotes the slide's message, accept it.

items.title: Multiple catches: ordering is a RULE
notes: Catch blocks are searched **in sequence**, and **only the first matching** one runs. A general catch also catches subclasses (IS-A).
Order: **most specific first, most general last**.
The slide calls it a 'Recommendation', but a superclass catch BEFORE a subclass catch is a **compile error** ('exception … has already been caught', verified).
Exam: `catch(Exception)` followed by `catch(ArithmeticException)` does **not compile**.

items.title: The nets analogy
notes: The small specific nets sit on top and catch the egg first. The big **General** net is last. If every net misses, the egg reaches the **JVM** and breaks (the program crashes with a trace).

items.title: Version 5: specific catch, then general catch, then finally
notes: `catch(ArithmeticException)` comes before `catch(Exception)`. Reversing them would not compile.
The ArithmeticException handler calls **`System.exit(0)`**, so **finally does NOT run** in that case.

items.title: System.exit skips finally (output proof)
notes: Case 0: prints only `Error: no of students must not equal to 0!`. There is **no** `End of program execution!`, because `System.exit(0)` in the catch stops the JVM before `finally`.
Case 5: `Average marks = 70.0` (the slide wrongly shows `70`) then `End of program execution!`.
Related (verified): if a catch block **throws** a new exception, `finally` still runs, and then the new exception propagates to the caller.

items.title: Creating your own exception class
notes: It must be **derived from an existing exception class**: `class IntNonNegativeException extends Exception`. That makes it **checked**. Extending RuntimeException would make it unchecked.
Usually you define **only constructors** that call `super(...)`: the no-arg one passes a default message, and the other passes the given `message`.
The slide says 'call the default constructor using super'. Really, `super("...")` calls `Exception(String)`.

items.title: Throw and catch your own exception in one method
notes: `throw new IntNonNegativeException();` uses the no-arg constructor, so `getMessage()` is `Integer input is a negative number!! `.
It is caught in the same method, so `getInteger()` needs no `throws` clause even though the exception is checked.
The catch calls `getIntAgain()` to retry.

items.title: Program output (negative input)
notes: Input 1,2,3,-2 then retry 4, then 5 gives sum `15`. The -2 is replaced by 4.
Small typo: the slide output says 'Enter total no. of **input** integers', but the code prints 'Enter total no. of integers'.

items.title: Second negative input terminates
notes: -2 triggers the exception, and the retry -4 makes `getIntAgain` print 2 error lines and call `System.exit(0)`. The sum is never printed.

items.title: Summary points
notes: Core advantage: exception handling **maintains the normal flow** of the application.
Without handling, an exception at statement 5 of 10 stops statements 6-10 from running. With handling, the rest can still run.
Its examples (ClassNotFound, IO, SQL, Remote) are all **checked** exceptions.
